explanation: Fires on a wide, mixed set of tokens: operators and punctuation in code and math (the '%' modulo operator, '{' in LaTeX fractions, ':' in Ruby symbols), digits inside version or OS strings (64-bit, jdk-13.0.1), '.twitter' in pic.twitter.com, and ordinary content words in prose (up, delay, types, affects, Document). No shared context explains these, so a new token is hard to predict.

Fires on verbs meaning to perform or carry out an activity: 'conduct'/'conducting' (strongest when followed by a study, test or operation), 'out' in 'carry out/carried out/carrying out', and 'perform'. It also fires on the 'conduct' piece of conductive/superconductivity. Weak on other light verbs (run, done, carried without 'out').

Diffuse. It fires on many words inside technical or scientific prose and code, often a noun naming a condition or factor (density, channel, pressure, serotonin, conditions, discharge) or a function word or punctuation right before one ('using key words', 'exposure to', 'your input', 'Copyright (C)'). No clear token-level or context-level rule.

Fires mostly in scientific or biomedical results text: on comparison words between numbers ('versus', '+/-', 'OR '), and on plural sample or study nouns (tissues, xenografts, isolates, transformants, patients, experiments, figures). Also fires on '/blob' in GitHub URLs and on 'to/with' after verbs of speaking or meeting ('journalists I spoke to'). A mixture.

Fires most strongly inside long runs of repeated characters or digits (zero-padded numbers like 000000053136, '8888, 999', runs of ';;;;'). It fires more weakly (~20-27%) on the 'func' keyword at the start of a Go function declaration, and on similar code keywords (var, import, Angular).

Fires mostly in license or copyright boilerplate: '(the "License")' in the Apache header, 'governing' in 'specific language governing permissions', 'Version' or the space before the version number, 'trademark of'. It also fires on some code-file starts (super, Object.defineProperty, def readme) and on scattered prose tokens. Strongest in formulaic legal or header text.

Mixed: it fires on closing parentheses and brackets in code or LaTeX, on operators in algebra word problems ('=', '+'), on words inside license text ('in all copies', 'at your option'), on 'as to', and on word pieces in prose, Japanese and Turkish. There is no unifying context.

Fires mostly on subword pieces and hyphens in the middle of a word, name or identifier, especially in non-English words, proper names or technical strings (l|ask|ussa, monat|lich, Tien Gi|ang, p,p'-DDE, moderate-to, grep -i, TH|OM|PKINS, PRE|CEDENTIAL). It also fires on some code tokens. Roughly 'continuation of a fragmented or unusual word', but noisy.

Fires on a heterogeneous set: attribute or module access in code (tf.nn, self.box), brackets and indices in MATLAB/VBA/Excel code (m(, [, A2, end), and assorted prose tokens (Congress, State, Discount, script, result). No common thread.

Fires on the head noun or object right after a verb or possessive in running prose (his comments, steer the country, the tale, the brand, take care of the bees). It also fires on some code tokens (filename, php://input). Weak and diffuse; hard to predict.

Fires on a semicolon that joins two clauses in prose (often before 'however', 'therefore', or a new clause), including in license text and 'text/html; charset'. It fires less on other clause-boundary tokens (relative 'that/who', '.', ','), so an ordinary sentence-final period gets only ~25%.

Fires on the '@' that opens a bracketed citation key in scientific text ('[@B9]', '([@bib29])', '[@ref5]'), strongest right after the sentence end or the opening parenthesis. It is weaker on later '@'s in a citation list, and fires on similar markup-delimiter tokens in code or templates ('%' in Jinja, '#' in anchors, '\' in LaTeX, '*').

Fires on 'class' in a Java/C#/Kotlin class declaration right after 'public'/'final'/'internal' (usually after imports), and on capital-letter acronym pieces (LRR, LPC, HMM, CMA, sauceLMS). It also fires on 'random order' / 'random access'. A mixture with code 'class' as the clearest part.

Fires on tokens in non-English, non-Latin-script text (Russian Cyrillic, Japanese katakana and kanji, Chinese) and on English text inside such documents. It also fires on scattered English prose and code tokens (there, ever, every, != , .execute). Strongest on the Russian and Japanese pieces, but the rest is diffuse.
